title: Cezar Capacle: Enhancing Narrative Through Randomness and Complications
speaker: Cezar Capacle
summary: Tabletop designer Cezar Capacle shares techniques from GM-less, 'anti-canon' tabletop RPGs where no lore is predefined and no game master prepares the world. He describes oracles — yes/no rolls and evocative random word prompts interpreted in context — and argues that humans' pattern-seeking turns random results into cohesive narrative, with a sweet spot balancing surprise and confirmed expectations. To keep stories moving without a GM he advocates fail-forward complications and Apocalypse World-style partial successes, a curated six-word complication oracle to avoid repetitive or runaway complications, and explicit mechanical procedures (even flowcharts) that provide 'structured randomness' without railroading story beats. In Q&A he distinguishes oracles from fixed random tables and describes curating evocative words.

insights.claim: GM-less, 'anti-canon' tabletop RPGs drop both a predefined world and a game master, generating lore during play collaboratively through in-game tools.
insights.detail: Capacle contrasts this with both railroad and sandbox adventures, which assume pre-existing lore and a GM who prepares everything. In his games, the world is at most brush strokes and nothing relies on a person bringing outside knowledge to fill gaps.
insights.quote: We have an anti-canon approach with no predefined lure. Lure is created, developed, and experienced as we play

insights.claim: An oracle replaces the game master by answering yes/no questions with probability-weighted rolls and open-ended questions with random evocative words that players interpret in context.
insights.detail: Yes/no questions ('is it raining?') use dice or cards modified by likelihood. Open-ended what/where/why/how questions use random word prompts that, like tarot cards, have no predefined interpretation. Treasure tables would require anticipating every interaction players might have.
insights.quote: The Oracle uses prompts or randomly selected words that work like tarot carts. They don't have predefined interpretation

insights.claim: Interpreting random word pairs in a story's context ties generated content to the specific character's narrative, as in rolling 'heal' and 'fear' for what's in a chest.
insights.detail: Using Mythic Game Master Emulator's meaning tables (d100), 'heal' and 'fear' could simply be a fear-curing potion; but for a character afraid of mimics, opening an empty chest safely could mean overcoming that fear.
insights.quote: That's the power of random words used in context as a definition tool

insights.claim: Random encounters and oracle results don't produce incoherent chaos because players' pattern-seeking and confirmation bias weave them into a cohesive narrative.
insights.detail: Capacle says cognitive biases harmful in real life — perceiving patterns in unrelated data and interpreting information to confirm expectations — are helpful when creating a story as you go; players even surprise themselves with their interpretations.
insights.quote: When we are faced with random Oracle results or encounters we tend to weave them into a cohesive narrative

insights.claim: The sweet spot for generated story results balances surprise with confirmed expectations, so a new revelation feels as if it had been foreshadowed.
insights.detail: When it works players say 'of course that's the answer' and feel satisfaction and cleverness at connecting earlier random events. He concludes random is not meaningless, and such stories can be more surprising than anything written in advance.
insights.quote: The sweet spot for me is offering a balance between surprise and confirming expectations

insights.claim: 'Fail forward' design makes even failures push the story onward by creating complications and new avenues rather than dead ends.
insights.detail: Stories thrive on drama built from conflict, which arises when characters don't get what they want. Old binary resolution meant a failed lock-pick roll just stalled the story; without a GM, tools are needed to push it forward.
insights.quote: Fail forward is a way to ensure that even when players fail a test or a role the narrative continues instead of offering stop block

insights.claim: Apocalypse World-style resolution has three bands — a miss means something unwanted happens, 7–9 is success with a cost or complication, 10+ is full success — and the partial-success band drives the story.
insights.detail: Capacle calls the 7–9 range the Goldilocks zone and names it the 'Indiana Jones effect': resolving one conflict creates the next, so after the inciting incident the rolls keep the story moving without injecting anything else. He says players land there most often.
insights.quote: 7-9 is a partial success where you get what you want but there is a cost, compromise or complication

insights.claim: Frequent partial successes become taxing: improvising complications can turn repetitive ('you get hurt') or pile up threats until the original mission is unrecognizable.
insights.detail: About a third of results land in the partial-success range, so players must constantly invent complications in long sessions.
insights.quote: Or it can get overly complex. You keep adding layers and layers of threats and story paths

insights.claim: A dedicated complication oracle of a few evocative verbs (break, harm, lose, escalate, drain, expose) with guiding keywords sits between pure random words and fixed complication lists.
insights.detail: Rolling 'escalate' on a failed lock-pick can be narrated as guards hearing a noise and dismissing it, adding looming tension without derailing the mission. This yields complications you wouldn't have thought of while avoiding repetitiveness.
insights.quote: a dedicated Oracle that lies in between random words and specific predetermined complications

insights.claim: Explicit play procedures, even flowcharts, create 'structured randomness' that tells players when to use oracles and complications, guiding mechanics without dictating story beats.
insights.detail: His flowchart: frame the scene, decide the complication, choose an approach, roll, conclude, repeat. He rebuts the concern that procedures are restrictive or board-game-like: they work at the mechanical level, not story level, and in his experience produce freer, more diverse storytelling and a game 'you can trust'.
insights.quote: the procedures work on the mechanical level not on the story level and guide you on how and when to use those shares

insights.claim: Oracles differ from random tables by giving open-to-interpretation words rather than hard-coded results, but can still be curated toward a theme, such as magic-effect words paired with mishap words.
insights.detail: In Q&A, Capacle contrasts a treasure table ('100 gold pieces, five sapphires') with an item oracle combining words like transparent, void, fire with corruption, decay, metamorphosis to define an item's power and its misuse risk.
insights.quote: That doesn't mean Oracles can't be curated even if they are not pre-specified results

insights.claim: Finding the right abstraction level for an evocative word list takes broad research and trial and error, filtering a large pool down to words between too broad and too specific.
insights.detail: Capacle cites Avery Alder's remark that design can be hours spent arriving at a list of 12 words. He compiled about 200 words from published games, videos and Reddit, then narrowed to six by discarding words too similar, too broad or too specific.
insights.quote: to create and curate six words on a random table it takes a week
